title: I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining.
author: Cengiz Yar
content:
Three summers ago, over Father’s Day weekend, my family and I went camping in
the Lincoln National Forest, just a few hours drive north of our home in El
Paso, Texas. It’s a beautiful area that’s long served as a getaway for the
region, with skiing in the winter, and golf and hiking in the summer. My
daughter played under the trees, and I rode my bike down mountain trails that,
I noticed, seemed concerningly dry.

The next evening, after we left to drive home, two fires started in forests
surrounding the town of Ruidoso, New Mexico, around 25 miles away from where
we’d been. I watched horrifying videos online of fire lapping the mountains
behind the village’s strip malls and parking lots. The fires were eventually
suppressed by a combination of human effort and the late summer monsoon
season. But when the downpour of rain hit the burnt landscape around Ruidoso,
it created another problem: Recurring floods then ripped through town,
damaging homes and infrastructure, and leading to emergency rescues.

The following summer, the scene repeated. On July 8, 2025, monsoon rain hit a
burn scar and quickly swelled the Rio Ruidoso and its tributaries. Three
people — two of them children — lost their lives.

Reporter Abe Streep, a member of ProPublica’s Southwest office, and I met in
Ruidoso to report on what happened. Ruidoso is a place built on tourism, with
a paid (rather than volunteer) fire department staff and its own disaster
manager. How could two children and a man be swept to their deaths in a place
that appeared equipped to handle such disasters?

In two stories ProPublica recently published, Abe answered those questions. He
found that, after the 2024 fires, [experts warned the town of increased flash
flooding risks](https://www.propublica.org/article/wildfire-flood-risk-
ruidoso-new-mexico). Initially, local and state leaders considered a
relocation plan for some homes and businesses that would get people out of
harm’s way, but the project faltered. Instead, village leaders continued
promoting tourism to the town, and the mayor even chastised residents for
warning of floods on social media. Abe also reported that, while local and
state officials insisted the emergency response to the flood was admirable,
[first responders say the three deaths could have been
avoided](https://www.propublica.org/article/ruidoso-flood-emergency-response-
water-rescue). The responders told Abe that village leadership left them
understaffed and inadequately equipped to contend with the flooding.

The Village of Ruidoso did not respond to detailed written questions about its
emergency response, and it has not publicly released a report on rescue
efforts during the flood. Reached by phone, the fire chief, Cade Hall,
disputed our reporting but declined to provide specifics. Mayor Lynn Crawford
has said protecting the village includes balancing public safety with tourism,
the lifeblood of its economy. But in an interview last year, Crawford said to
Abe and me: “Who’s to blame? I didn’t start the fire.”

My role as a photographer was to document Ruidoso as the story unfolded — to
visualize the people and place at the center of it. It’s a role I’ve had
countless times in my career, but this story hit unexpectedly close to home. I
could imagine my own family caught unaware in a similar situation, trying to
escape the El Paso summer heat but instead navigating an unfathomable
disaster.

![A severely damaged home rests tilted and collapsed amid thick mud, dirt
mounds and scattered structural debris in a heavily flooded
area.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso3-9_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)A
crumbled trailer and debris from flash flooding in Ruidoso on Aug. 1, 2025
![The structural ruins of a partially collapsed house with a damaged metal
roof, exposed wooden framing and piled cinder blocks among tall pine
trees.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso3-11_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)The
crumbling house at the Riverview RV Park on Sept. 10, 2026

When Abe and I started reporting, we met people from the community and out of
town who tried to help. I watched as New Mexico National Guard service members
loaded sand bags into families’ cars, people prepared hot meals for those who
had been displaced and volunteers handed out donated supplies from collection
centers.

![Pallets stacked with relief supplies, including bulk cases of baby diapers,
wipes and cardboard boxes, fill a staging warehouse area alongside a red
pallet jack, plastic laundry baskets and storage
totes.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso3-8_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)
![A tracked skid steer loader lifts a pallet of white sandbags at a
preparation site, with the Ruidoso Downs Race Track & Casino sign visible in
the background.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso3-7_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)

Supplies inside a Salvation Army makeshift distribution center and a sandbag
distribution point facilitated by the New Mexico National Guard last summer

While we were reporting one afternoon, it started raining. Fear swept through
me. Our phones lit up with flood warnings from the National Weather Service.
We knew we should take them seriously.

Abe and I sought refuge in a local brewery perched high above the river basin.
Before we knew it, the water from that thin little creek of Rio Ruidoso became
a torrent. The rushing water rose quickly. It swept through the river valley
right under the brewery, carrying what looked like trees and debris with it.

![A woman stands indoors looking out a rain-streaked window toward a swollen,
muddy river flowing through a wooded residential
valley.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso3-6_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)A
woman watches the Rio Ruidoso rise from inside a brewery in downtown Ruidoso
last summer. ![People stand along a wet road observing a swollen, muddy river
flowing past a red house surrounded by flood debris and fallen
trees.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso3-5_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)Two
people venture close to the river as a flash flood began to subside last
summer.

Still, I wanted to photograph the river up close. I left the safety of the
brewery and let the heavy rain cover me as I moved closer to the river. As I
made photos that afternoon and throughout the rest of the trip, questions
about my own safety ran through my mind: Would the water keep rising? If it
did, could I get to high ground? And, notably, would I have enough warning?

In hindsight, I realize these questions were largely about whether I could
trust the systems in place to keep me and others safe. And as Abe kept
reporting over the next year, the more those questions felt valid.

Last month, Abe and I traveled again to Ruidoso. The town felt lighter and
less ominous. Much of the ruin had been removed or rebuilt. Grass and
sagebrush sprouted on a burn scar. Tourists wandered around a lively downtown
on a Friday afternoon. People seemed to be moving on from the terror of the
previous year.

![Pedestrians cross a street in downtown Ruidoso, with an adobe building
painted with a “Ruidoso, New Mexico — Sierra Blanca” mountain mural in the
background.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso3-4_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)Downtown
Ruidoso on a Friday afternoon this summer ![A young deer walks past an adult
elk standing in a grassy clearing with a pine forest in the
background.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso3-3_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)A
mule deer and an elk wander behind downtown Ruidoso. ![A large pile of
cleared, fallen tree trunks rests in the foreground of a grassy field, with a
rolling, sparse hill stretching into the background under a pale
sky.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso3-2_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)New
growth on a burn scar above Ruidoso

But Stephanie and Sebastian Trotter still carry the scars of the day. They
lost their two children, Sebastian Rowan, 7, and Charlotte, 4, in the Ruidoso
flooding.

There is now a memorial for them and Benjamin “Tim” Feagin, the third person
who died, at the RV park where they had been camped. But I wanted to see for
myself the places where each of them was found. I felt that making photos of
those places could help people connect with the reality of their deaths as
well as their lives. So, early one morning, I walked along the floodplain
trying to find the locations Abe had shared with me.

I got to the bridge where a firefighter found Sebastian Rowan. There was no
marker, no indication that anyone’s body had been found there.

Then I went looking for the area where Charlotte was found. I wandered under
pine and cottonwood, through knee-deep grasses and wild sunflowers. Crows
cawed overhead, and the early morning sun broke through the trees. I stood
there for a while, admiring the beauty, awed by the sadness of the river’s
trickle.

![Sunlight reflects off a calm, shallow stream winding through a quiet, shaded
woodland area flanked by trees and exposed
roots.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/2026-CengizYar-
Ruidoso3-1_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=2560)Rio
Ruidoso, near where the body of Sebastian Rowan was found
